\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all generation depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking schemes \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} require proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively to existing corpora.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterizes how recursive training degrades model quality but assumes the generation depth is known a priori---the very quantity we seek to estimate.
\citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} show that filtering synthetic data from training corpora can prevent collapse, yet their approach relies on binary detection and does not distinguish among recursive depths.
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the extent of single-pass editing applied to a text but does not address multi-step recursive generation.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints exhibit universal stability across model families and decoding strategies.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by Gini importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all generation depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking schemes \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} require proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively to existing corpora.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterizes how recursive training degrades model quality but assumes the generation depth is known a priori---the very quantity we seek to estimate.
\citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} show that filtering synthetic data from training corpora can prevent collapse, yet their approach relies on binary detection and does not distinguish among recursive depths.
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the extent of single-pass editing applied to a text but does not address multi-step recursive generation.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints exhibit universal stability across model families and decoding strategies.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).

\subsection{End-to-End Learning}
\label{sec:gen:dcol}

We test whether end-to-end finetuning can bypass feature engineering.
We train DeBERTa-v3-base and RoBERTa-base with standard hyperparameters (lr$\,{=}\,2{\times}10^{-5}$, 3 epochs, batch 16, max 512 tokens, 5-fold CV) on the Pythia-1.4B nucleus data.
Both achieve ${\sim}$59\% accuracy (DeBERTa 58.3$\pm$4.7\%, RoBERTa 59.5$\pm$3.2\%), substantially below feature-based classifiers (78.2\%, gap ${\approx}$19pp).
Both transformers easily distinguish human from machine text (d0 F1$>$0.95) but fail at adjacent-depth discrimination (d1/d2 F1$<$0.42), precisely where statistical features like \textsc{p90\_ppl} and \textsc{var\_surprisal} excel.
The architecture-invariant gap (1.2pp between backbones) rules out model selection bias and confirms that hand-crafted statistical features capture depth-discriminative signals that end-to-end finetuning cannot recover from raw text alone.

We additionally tested Deep Contrastive Ordinal Learning (DCOL) with a RoBERTa-large encoder; across six configurations, five suffered training instabilities (embedding collapse, OOM, gradient explosion) and the best run reached only 64.5\% with severe overfitting.
While ordinal contrastive methods such as CLOC \cite{cloc2025} show promise for continuous ordinal targets, the discrete and compressing nature of recursive depth resists end-to-end extraction.

\paragraph{Feature overlap analysis.}
Probing analysis reveals a significant negative correlation between DeBERTa attention-based feature importance and RF permutation importance (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.484$, $p{=}0.036$), with zero overlap in top-5 features (Jaccard$\,{=}\,0.0$).
DeBERTa attends to surface-level lexical patterns (type--token ratio, repeated bigrams, bigram entropy), while RF relies on perplexity distribution statistics (\textsc{var\_surprisal}, \textsc{p90\_ppl}, skewness).
This complementarity confirms that transformer representations are biased toward lexical and repetition patterns, missing the high-order perplexity tail statistics that carry depth signal.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursively training language models on their own outputs erodes distributional tails, eventually collapsing the output distribution to a narrow mode.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this phenomenon through scaling laws that distinguish tail \emph{narrowing} (reduced variance) from tail \emph{cutting} (lost support), showing both accelerate with recursion depth; \citet{dohmatob2024_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and \citet{dohmatob2024_demystified} analyze the regression case.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this analysis to self-consuming generative models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff as synthetic data accumulates across generations.
\citet{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} show that retaining real data alongside synthetic data across generations mitigates collapse, while \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} demonstrate that filtering synthetic samples via binary detection can preserve model quality.
Recent work further refines the theoretical picture: \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} identify non-monotonic dynamics where early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality before eventual degradation; \citet{marchi2024_heat_death} characterize convergence to a fixed-point ``heat death'' distribution; and \citet{wang2026_contamination} derive contamination guarantees bounding how much synthetic data a corpus can absorb.
Additional lines of work address curated synthetic pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse in factual recall \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures of model-generated text \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and the ``synthetic eggs'' problem in self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation patterns but assume the generation depth is known a priori; our work addresses the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature---the tendency of model-generated text to occupy local maxima of the log-probability surface---as a zero-shot detection signal.
\citet{fast_detectgpt2024} improve computational efficiency by replacing random perturbations with conditional probability curvature from a surrogate model.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits the perplexity ratio between two related models, achieving strong detection without training data.
DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity patterns, while GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} provides statistical visualization of per-token likelihood ranks for human inspection.
\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} expose fundamental limits: paraphrasing attacks reduce detection accuracy to near chance, and \citet{pudasaini2026_detection_fails} show detection degrades under distribution shift between training and deployment domains.
\citet{pu2026_generator_barrier} formalize a generator barrier bounding detection performance when the generator is unknown.
All these methods perform binary classification (human vs.\ machine), discarding the ordinal depth information that distinguishes first-generation from deeply recursive text.
Our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the \emph{extent} of editing applied to a passage---a continuous measure of how much a text has been modified in a single pass---but does not model recursive generation chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} formulate authorship attribution as multi-source classification, identifying \emph{which} model generated a text rather than \emph{how many} recursive steps it has undergone.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} provides a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple synthetic data modalities but evaluates binary detection, not depth estimation.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, quantifying information distortion across rounds; while their work measures forward degradation fidelity, our task performs the inverse: classifying generation depth from text alone, without access to the generation chain.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
The choice of decoding strategy shapes the statistical properties of generated text in ways that interact with recursive depth signals.
\citet{holtzman2020_nucleus} show that unrestricted sampling produces degenerate repetitions and propose nucleus sampling to maintain output diversity.
\citet{finlayson2024_closing} demonstrate that decoding parameters affect downstream evaluation metrics in non-trivial ways.
\citet{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded} find that the effect of decoding strategies on text quality is model-dependent, complicating universal quality claims.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} provide a systematic comparison of decoding methods on surface-level text properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} introduces perplexity-controlled decoding that actively regulates output entropy.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects that go beyond single-pass text quality to shape the discriminability of recursive depth itself.

\subsection{Effective Discriminable Depth}
\label{sec:atlas:edd}

Aggregate accuracy masks the fact that adjacent depths become harder to distinguish as depth increases.
We quantify this via the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD).
For each adjacent depth pair $(d, d{+}1)$, we train a dedicated binary RF (500 trees, 5-fold stratified CV) and compute $\mathrm{AUC}(d, d{+}1)$---the ROC AUC of this pairwise classifier at separating depth-$d$ from depth-$(d{+}1)$ samples.
Given a discrimination threshold $T$, EDD is defined as:
\[
\mathrm{EDD}_T = \max \bigl\{ d^*{+}1 : \mathrm{AUC}(d^*, d^*{+}1) \geq T \bigr\}
\]
where $d^* \in \{0, 1, \dots, K{-}1\}$.
Intuitively, $\mathrm{EDD}_T$ is the deepest generation depth at which the classifier can still reliably separate it from the preceding depth; beyond this boundary, adjacent depths become statistically indistinguishable.
We set $T{=}0.75$ as the default threshold---the midpoint between chance AUC (0.5) and perfect discrimination (1.0)---and report sensitivity at $T \in \{0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80\}$ below.

Within the 4-class atlas (d0--d3), 7 of 9 cells achieve $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=3$; the two exceptions are Pythia and OLMo with top-$k$ sampling ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=2$), consistent with top-$k$'s signal-attenuating effect noted in \S\ref{sec:atlas:indist}.

To probe deeper, we extend the Pythia-1.4B nucleus pipeline to 6 depths (d0--d5) and train a 500-tree binary RF for each adjacent pair (we increase from 200 to 500 trees for binary classifiers to ensure convergence on the smaller per-pair sample sizes).
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} shows the pairwise AUC decay curve.
The d0\,vs.\,d1 boundary is near-perfect (AUC\,=\,0.998), reflecting the well-known human--machine gap.
Subsequent boundaries degrade monotonically: d1\,vs.\,d2 achieves 0.925 [95\% CI: 0.914,\,0.935], d2\,vs.\,d3 reaches 0.823 [0.805,\,0.840], and d3\,vs.\,d4 yields 0.784 [0.765,\,0.802]---with the confidence interval lower bound still exceeding $T{=}0.75$.
At d4\,vs.\,d5, AUC drops to 0.683 [0.661,\,0.705], falling below the threshold and fixing $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}=4$.

\paragraph{Z-score normalization does not resolve the inversion.}
A natural hypothesis is that per-feature z-score normalization might correct this covariate shift \cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting}.
For RF, z-normalization leaves accuracy essentially unchanged (59.1\% $\to$ 59.2\%) and does not improve d1v2 AUC ($\Delta < 0.02$), as expected since tree splits depend on feature rank order, not scale.
Z-score standardization improves overall logistic regression cross-strategy accuracy from 25\% to 61\%, with d1v2 AUC gains for nucleus and top-$k$ holdouts (0.61--0.89).
However, it does not recover the temperature-induced d1v2 inversion---AUC worsens for two of three models (GPT-2~XL 0.50$\to$0.24, OLMo 0.50$\to$0.19; Pythia 0.52), confirming that temperature decoding induces a genuine geometry-level shift in feature space rather than a correctable scale difference.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all generation depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking schemes \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} require proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively to existing corpora.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterizes how recursive training degrades model quality but assumes the generation depth is known a priori---the very quantity we seek to estimate.
\citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} show that filtering synthetic data from training corpora can prevent collapse, yet their approach relies on binary detection and does not distinguish among recursive depths.
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the extent of single-pass editing applied to a text but does not address multi-step recursive generation.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints exhibit universal stability across model families and decoding strategies.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a 19-dimensional feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, distinguishing it from binary detection and single-pass editing estimation. We introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells (100\%) and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 7/9 (78\%), with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. The extended Pythia nucleus pipeline (d0--d5) yields $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$, establishing that depth discrimination persists through four recursive steps before falling below threshold.

    \item \textbf{Generalization analysis.} Cross-model leave-one-out transfer achieves 66.4\% mean accuracy and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\% (chance = 25\%), demonstrating partial universality of depth fingerprints. We identify a temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion (GPT-2~XL: 0.13, OLMo: 0.25) caused by accelerated convergence. Z-score normalization improves overall LR cross-strategy accuracy (25\%$\to$61\%) but does not recover the temperature-induced d1/d2 inversion (GPT-2~XL 0.50$\to$0.24, OLMo 0.50$\to$0.19), confirming a genuine geometry-level shift rather than a correctable scale difference.

    \item \textbf{End-to-end learning as negative result.} Both DeBERTa-v3-base (58.3\%) and RoBERTa-base (59.5\%) achieve ${\sim}$59\% via end-to-end finetuning---19pp below feature-based classifiers (78.2\%)---with the architecture-invariant gap ruling out model selection bias. Probing reveals a significant negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.48$) between transformer attention and RF feature importance, confirming complementary representations.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Model Collapse Theory.}
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} demonstrate that recursively training language models on their own outputs erodes distributional tails, eventually collapsing the output distribution to a narrow mode.
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} formalize this phenomenon through scaling laws that distinguish tail \emph{narrowing} (reduced variance) from tail \emph{cutting} (lost support), showing both accelerate with recursion depth; \citet{dohmatob2024_strong_collapse} establish strong collapse guarantees, and \citet{dohmatob2024_demystified} analyze the regression case.
The MAD framework \cite{alemohammad2024_mad} extends this analysis to self-consuming generative models and quantifies the precision--recall tradeoff as synthetic data accumulates across generations.
Mitigation strategies include retaining real data \cite{gerstgrasser2024_accumulate} and filtering synthetic samples via detection \cite{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse}.
Recent work identifies non-monotonic dynamics \cite{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement}, fixed-point convergence \cite{marchi2024_heat_death}, contamination bounds \cite{wang2026_contamination}, curated pipelines \cite{falahati2026_curated}, knowledge collapse \cite{knowledge_collapse2025}, spectral signatures \cite{sigma2026_spectral}, and self-improving loops \cite{synthetic_eggs2026}.
These works characterize degradation patterns but assume the generation depth is known a priori; our work addresses the inverse problem of estimating depth from text alone.

\paragraph{AI Text Detection.}
DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} introduced probability curvature---the tendency of model-generated text to occupy local maxima of the log-probability surface---as a zero-shot detection signal.
\citet{fast_detectgpt2024} improve computational efficiency by replacing random perturbations with conditional probability curvature from a surrogate model.
Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024} exploits the perplexity ratio between two related models, achieving strong detection without training data.
DivEye \cite{diveye2026} leverages surprisal diversity patterns, while GLTR \cite{gehrmann2019_gltr} provides statistical visualization of per-token likelihood ranks for human inspection.
\citet{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} expose fundamental limits: paraphrasing attacks reduce detection accuracy to near chance, and \citet{pudasaini2026_detection_fails} show detection degrades under distribution shift between training and deployment domains.
\citet{pu2026_generator_barrier} formalize a generator barrier bounding detection performance when the generator is unknown.
All these methods perform binary classification (human vs.\ machine), discarding the ordinal depth information that distinguishes first-generation from deeply recursive text.
Our approach outputs ordinal depth labels, complementing rather than replacing binary detection.

\paragraph{Adjacent Tasks.}
EditLens \cite{editlens2026} estimates the \emph{extent} of editing applied to a passage---a continuous measure of how much a text has been modified in a single pass---but does not model recursive generation chains.
\citet{uchendu2020_attribution} formulate authorship attribution as multi-source classification, identifying \emph{which} model generated a text rather than \emph{how many} recursive steps it has undergone.
LOKI \cite{loki2025} provides a comprehensive benchmark spanning multiple synthetic data modalities but evaluates binary detection, not depth estimation.
\citet{mohamed2025_broken_telephone} study iterative generation as a ``broken telephone'' effect, quantifying information distortion across rounds; while their work measures forward degradation fidelity, our task performs the inverse: classifying generation depth from text alone, without access to the generation chain.

\paragraph{Decoding Strategy Effects.}
The choice of decoding strategy shapes the statistical properties of generated text in ways that interact with recursive depth signals.
\citet{holtzman2020_nucleus} show that unrestricted sampling produces degenerate repetitions and propose nucleus sampling to maintain output diversity.
\citet{finlayson2024_closing} demonstrate that decoding parameters affect downstream evaluation metrics in non-trivial ways.
\citet{garces_arias2025_decoding_decoded} find that the effect of decoding strategies on text quality is model-dependent, complicating universal quality claims.
\citet{wiher2022_decoding} provide a systematic comparison of decoding methods on surface-level text properties, and Mirostat \cite{basu2021_mirostat} introduces perplexity-controlled decoding that actively regulates output entropy.
Our Depth Degradation Atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas}) reveals that these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation---temperature sampling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---effects that go beyond single-pass text quality to shape the discriminability of recursive depth itself.

\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract 19 statistical features---perplexity percentiles, surprisal moments, and lexical diversity measures---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 40\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as universal depth markers (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 7/9 model--strategy cells, respectively; mean Spearman $\rho{=}0.868$).
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%, though temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that z-score normalization cannot resolve.
\end{abstract}
